name_en: Da Bai Cultivar White Tea (Fuding Dabai, Dahao, Zhenghe Dabai)
cultivar: Fuding Dabai (Huacha 1), Fuding Dahao (Huacha 2), Zhenghe Dabai
processing: The standard white-tea process of withering and low-temperature drying applied to the big, downy shoots of the Dabai and Dahao bushes; the cultivar determines bud size, down, timing and the tea's basic character more than the maker does.
harvest_season: Fuding Dabai and Dahao bud early, from mid or late March; Zhenghe Dabai is roughly two weeks later. All three are picked in spring for the fine grades and in autumn for Shou Mei.
appearance_dry: Dahao: the fattest, most heavily downed buds; Fuding Dabai: slightly slimmer and finer; Zhenghe Dabai: long, slender, greyer buds.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold in all three, Zhenghe a shade deeper.
appearance_wet: Large, soft, pale buds and leaves; Zhenghe's are longer and narrower.
taste_profile: Dahao is sweet, soft and creamy; Fuding Dabai is more aromatic and refined; Zhenghe Dabai is deeper, more savoury and longer in the finish.

brewing.notes: Brew as for any white tea of the same grade; the cultivar shows most in the texture and the finish.

vintage_note: Not a product in itself but the cultivar behind nearly all Fujian white tea, sold fresh (current spring) or aged (cakes with a year). Labels rarely state the cultivar; when they do, Dahao usually means a plumper, cheaper, high-yield tea, Fuding Dabai a more aromatic one, Zhenghe Dabai a deeper one. 'Da Bai' in a product name also often just means 'from Fuding'.
description:
The reason northern Fujian can make a tea out of nothing but buds is the bushes. Three cultivars, Fuding Dabai, Fuding Dahao and Zhenghe Dabai, were selected from local seedlings in the 1800s and early 1900s, propagated by cuttings and spread across the two counties, and their large, downy, early buds are what every Silver Needle and Mudan is made from. 'Da bai' means 'big white' and refers to the bud, not to the tea category.

Fuding Dabai, registered nationally as Huacha 1, is the original: early-budding, downy, refined in aroma. Fuding Dahao, Huacha 2, is its bigger, hairier, higher-yielding sibling, and because it produces fatter buds and more of them, it now makes most of the Silver Needle on the market. Zhenghe Dabai, from the inland county, buds about two weeks later and grows long, slender buds with more amino acids and a deeper flavour. The same bushes also supply the base for Fujian jasmine teas, Bai Lin Gongfu black tea and some greens.

In the cup, with the same grade and maker, Dahao is the softest and creamiest, sweet and easy; Fuding Dabai is more fragrant and precise; Zhenghe Dabai is fuller, more savoury and longer. The difference is a matter of degree, not of kind, but it is real, and it explains why a Zhenghe Silver Needle looks and tastes different from a Fuding one even when both are perfectly made.

You will rarely see the cultivar on a Western label, and in China 'Da Bai' in a product name often just signals Fuding origin. When a seller does specify, Dahao usually means a plumper, cheaper tea, Dabai a more aromatic one at a premium, and Zhenghe Dabai a deeper one. The small-leaf, seed-grown Cai Cha bushes are the fourth option, giving smaller, more characterful shoots for Gong Mei. None of this changes the basic buying rules: county, grade, picking date, and year if aged.

If a seller offers a Fuding Dabai and a Dahao Silver Needle from the same spring, buy both; it is a rare chance to taste the cultivar on its own.
sources_note: Cultivar card. Origin dates ('1800s and early 1900s') follow local records as usually cited (Fuding Dabai c. 1857, Fuding Dahao c. 1880s, Zhenghe Dabai c. 1880s); the national registration numbers Huacha 1 and 2 are as commonly given.
